# Abstract

<!--# Ca. 150 words -->

Stratigraphic paleobiology seeks to understand how physical processes shape the fossil record, whereas phylogenetics seeks to reconstruct evolutionary relationships, rates, and mechanisms. Stratigraphy, the science of Earth's history, is the key source of time information in phylogenies and reconstructed evolutionary trees allow us to fill gaps in the fossil record. Yet, few studies exploit both approaches simultaneously. The challenge of reconciling physical geological record with phylogenetics lies in theoretical chasms between disciplines, computational tools available to researchers, technical skills, and ontologies of uncertainty. Meanwhile recent advances in modelling in both areas create opportunities for joint models of stratigraphic and phylogenetic processes. In this workshop, we will isolate these opportunities and invite stratigraphers, evolutionary biologists and software engineers to solve them together interactively. This workshops aims to establish a workflow for incorporating geological record in phylogenetic inference, to create a roadmap for digital infrastructure required for successful integration of geological and evolutionary data, and to translate these theoretical advances into actionable research software improvements.

**Phylogenetics** is the science of reconstructing evolutionary relationships, rates and processes. It is built through a concerted effort of mathematicians, palaeobiologists, geneticists, and computer scientists. For decades, the primary source of data for phylogenetic trees and the methods used to infer them were genetic sequences from living and - in exceptional circumstances - recently extinct taxa. Such data represents a tip-of-an-iceberg proportion of known diversity, as over 99% of organisms are extinct and either discovereable as **fossils** or lost for good. For many reasons, which can be argued mathematically and are understood intuitively, inclusion of fossils in phylogenetic trees, regardless of the methodological extent, radically improves our reconstruction of evolution (@ronquist_total-evidence_2012, @gavryushkina_bayesian_2017; @saladin_fossils_2017). 

The recent mathematical development known as the **Fossilized Birth-Death** (FBD) family of models treats fossils and extant species as observations from the same macroevolutionary process, rather than external calibration constraints, providing statistically principled methods for integrating temporal, morphological, and molecular evidence. The introduction of the FBD process has led to major revisions in evolutionary timelines across diverse groups from insects to mammals, demonstrating that fossil data contains irreplaceable information about deep-time evolutionary processes. 

Among the features of the FBD model that allow it to incorporate fossil data is the fact that (1) it is a diversification and **sampling model** and (2) the inference of the topology can include fossil ages (@wright_integrating_2022). These two aspects of the FBD model, sampling and fossil ages, constitute the interface between phylogenetics and geosciences. Phylogeneticists have acutely experienced the detrimental effects of using fossil ages without sufficient context (@ronquist_total-evidence_2012). Fossils can virtually never be dated directly and the typical precision of a fossil age is several million years. Ignoring stratigraphic age uncertainty, which can introduce errors of 10-20 million years in divergence time estimates [@barido-sottani_ignoring_2020]

**Stratigraphic paleobiology** is the discipline studying the laws and processes governing fossil preservation and discoverability. It offers a theoretical framework and a predictive toolbox for identifying gaps in the fossil record, environmental factors affecting fossil occurrences, and quantification of the uncertainty of fossil ages (@patzkowsky_stratigraphic_2012). In this workshop we aim to address challenges of using fossil data in phylogenies using the stratigraphic palaeobiology approach.

## Research challenges of the field

### Understanding the geological record

The geological record offers a conceptual challenge: it can be represented in the stratigraphic (depth) domain and in the time domain. The stratigraphic domain is the physical record: the strata, the fossils, the boundaries and event horizons, the minerals bearing radioisotopes that allow calibration in absolute time. The time domain is where the strata and fossils are formed, where extinction and originations happen, and what we cannot observe but must reconstruct from the stratigraphic domain. Most information needed for phylogenetics is implicitly expressed in the time domain (fossil ages, rates, sampling), but taken from the stratigraphic domain. The stratigraphic record is commonly treated as a continuous, lossless mapping from the time domain, but the broad and diverse fields of stratigraphy and sedimentology provide a wealth of processes that challenge this approach. Recent advances in modeling and geochronology allow us to build representations of time in geological strata, including their uncertainty (@hohmann_nonparametric_2024). They also show that gaps in the stratigraphic record do not necessarily compromise the recovery of evolutionary processes (@hohmann_identification_2024).

### Models of morphological evolution

Beyond providing temporal information, fossils also preserve morphological characteristics in their appearance, which provide an important souce of data for phylogenetic inference. The use of discretized morphological data in phylogenetics has traditionally relied on parsimony-based methods. More recently, however, their application within a Bayesian framework has gained traction, offering the advantage of directly incorporating fossil data into time-calibrated phylogenetic inference while jointly resolving relationships among both extinct and extant lineages @wright2014. Nevertheless, the number of morphological models available to describe character change remains limited, reflecting the difficulty of generalizing trait evolution. The most widely used approach is the Mk model, which assumes equal transition rates among states and equal stationary frequencies @lewis2001. Several extensions of this model have been developed and are frequently applied, although their assumptions about character evolution remain relatively simplistic. Despite these limitations, studies indicate that such models perform well and are capable of capturing essential aspects of the evolutionary process @mulvey2025. An important aspect of fossil character data that remains underexplored is the influence of stratigraphic and taphonomic biases, both on the fossils themselves and on the loss of entire specimens from the fossil record. Gaining a better understanding of how these biases shape our observed data could inform strategies to model the processes that generated it, integrating insights from both biological and geological perspectives.

### Interdisciplinarity

Fossil data used for phylogenetic tree inference is qualitatively different from genetic (also referred to as molecular) data used for modern organisms. The dynamics of molecular evolution is arguably much better understood and allows for easier comparison between distantly related groups of organisms. A molecular phylogenicist can rapidly familiarise themselves with genetic data for a new group. In contrast, fossils are almost exclusively known from their (usually skeletal) morphological remains, often fragmentary, which require expert knowledge of anatomy, preservation and geological sampling to translate into data useful for phylogenetics. Yet, meta-analyses of combined molecular-morphological datasets demonstrate that morphological and molecular information on the same sets of organisms frequently show conflicting signals when analyzed separately, but combined analyses often yield unique trees not sampled by either type of information (partition) individually (@keating_phylogenetic_2023). Even when morphological data has a lower information contents on its own, it consistently improves phylogenetic resolution and accuracy when combined with molecular data (@asher_phylogenetic_2022). Empowering phylogeneticists to use the wealth of fossil data requires not only development and validation of models of morphological evolution, but also breaking the disciplinary ice and an in-depth dialogue.

## Aims of the workshop

Our goal is to achieve an integration of phylogenetics and stratigraphic palaeobiology, communicate it to the scientific community through a publication, and foster collaboration between scientists contributing to both fields, helping them overcome the disciplinary boundaries.

## Workshop outcomes

### Short-term impact

At the end of the workshop, we will have produced:

1.  A **best-practices recommendations list** for publishing and reviewing phylogenetic analyses and reporting fossil and stratigraphic information.
2.  A **roadmap for digital infrastructure** needed for landmark use-cases of phylogenetic analysis incorporating fossil data
3.  A **technical draft of a phylogenetic reconstruction from simulated data**, addressing uncertainties, sources of error, and instructions for practitioners - this draft will become the basis for a future publication and tutorial

We will also have **trained** and **built capacity** in using methods of the respective disciplines among phylogeneticists interested in incorporating geological knowledge and stratgraphic palaeobiologists aiming to bring in their expertise into phylogenetics.

### Long-term impact

1.  A chapter on using fossil and stratigraphic data in phylogenetic analyses and on replicability in a new planned article on best practices
2.  Translation of researcher needs into digital infrastructure: based on the roadmap for digital infrastructure, feature requests including specifications of missing parts of algorithms and documentation will be prepared, following best practices in research software design. This will allow matching software capabilities with scientific needs and will ensure proper validation of the complex computations involved in phylogenetic inference.
3.  A scientific article on phylogenetic inference from incomplete (gappy) fossil data and on incorporating stratigraphic precision and accuracy.

# Program

Each day will be dedicated to one problem, to reduce cognitive load, and led by one of the organizers.

## Monday: the structure of the geological record

*Emilia Jarochowska*

**Lorentz Center welcome and opening**

Introductory lecture by Mark Patzkowsky: **Principles of Stratigraphic Palaeobiology**

**Ice-breaker workshop: Make your own geological record.** In a pre-workshop survey we will ask participants about their coding skills and divide them into "novice", "familiar" and "expert". In the workshop, we will make sure that novice users are always paired with experts and that senior researchers are paired with ECRs. In this workshop, participants will learn the basics of creating a simple model of the geological record on their own computers. This exercise has been tested in two previous workshops and is suitable for a diverse audience.

In-depth lecture by Lydian Boschman: **Palaeogeography and plate tectonics in phylogenies**

Diving deep workshop: **Extracting information for phylogenies from strata**. We will use the models created in the morning to extract information which can be used in phylogenetic analyses: age-depth models, fossil ranges including their uncertainties, apparent origination and extionction rates. These datasets will be used in the following days.

**Welcome reception**

## Tuesday: Models of morphological evolution

*Laura Mulvey*

To Be Filled

## Wednesday: Tree inference from fossil data

*Niklas Hohmann*

To Be Filled

**Evening: Workshop dinner**

## Thursday: Best practices and replicability? Validation between RB and BEAST?

*Rachel Warnock*

To Be Filled

Maybe a good day to include other modalities: brainstorms, breakout rooms?

## Friday: Interactive synthesis

*Everyone*

*Caution: this day needs to end by 15:30 latest*

We will dedicate the day to carrying out a hands-on phylogenetic analyses representing two common scenarios: tree inference from incomplete geological record using the FBD Skyline model and tree inference accounting for fossil occurrence uncertainty using the FBD Range model. We will use simulated data of which we have perfect knowledge and the goal will be to recover the original tree properties.

We will apply the *literate programming* approach: documenting our work in human language alongside code. The created document will be the basis for a scientific publication, as well as a tutorial for other users. We will again make sure to pair members with different expertise, i.e. self-declared experts with novices.

Due to high computation time of the analyses they may not be finished by the end of the workshop, although we will provide SURF computing infrastructure to ensure as rapid completion as possible. We will finish the day and the workshop with a joint revision of what has been achieved. To this goal, we will offer the ECRs to present a summary of the reconstruction and the results (if already available) on behalf of their teams and to be the ambassadors of the respective team's concerns, recommendations, and findings.

# Participants

We aim the workshop at participants with prior experience with phylogenetics, even if they are at the beginning of a PhD journey, and a small number of key participants representing stratigraphic palaeobiology. Since digital infrastructure is among the challenges in this field, we target particularly participants with at least an intention to engage with the software or research software engineers and to discuss the interplay between the needs of the users and the computational possibilities. 

Since the workshop will include hands-on sessions, including writing or running simple code (with ample help and instruction from the organizers), we intend to survey the participants about their skills and assign them to groups with mixed background, so they can work on problems together.
